title: Spectral Audio Signal Processing — shard 2: Chapters 5–7 (Spectrum Analysis of Sinusoids through Time-Frequency Displays)
access: full (official freely readable Stanford CCRMA linked-HTML edition; cited as Julius O. Smith III, W3K Publishing, 2011, ISBN 978-0-9745607-3-1; the maintained pages display a 2026-06-10 copyright footer and no broad image-reuse license)
topics: Chapter 5, Spectrum Analysis of Sinusoids: why short-time sinusoidal peaks are compact models for tonal audio, additive synthesis, model calibration, pitch estimation, source grouping, selected-source modification, and noise reduction.

§5.1, Spectrum of a Sinusoid: amplitude, phase, radian/Hz frequency, decomposition of a real sinusoid into positive- and negative-frequency complex exponentials, analytic signal, and the impulse-pair Fourier spectrum.
§5.2, Spectrum of a Sampled Complex Sinusoid: normalized radian frequency, discrete-time complex exponentials, and the periodic DTFT impulse representation.

§5.3, Spectrum of a Windowed Sinusoid: finite observation as time-domain windowing, rectangular versus tapered windows, zero-centered and causal forms, and the linear phase introduced by shifting a window.

§5.4, Effect of Windowing: multiplication/convolution duality, the sinusoid becoming a shifted and scaled window transform, main-lobe smearing, sidelobe leakage, and competing definitions of an optimal analysis window.
§5.4.1, Frequency Resolution: main-lobe width as the resolution control, the rectangular window as the narrowest-main-lobe choice, and dependence on window length.

§5.4.1 examples, Two In-Phase Cosines and Phase-Quadrature Sine/Cosine: controlled window-length experiments showing apparent resolution, amplitude/frequency bias, and sensitivity to relative phase when peaks overlap.
§5.5, Resolving Sinusoids: zero-crossing, moment, and engineering definitions of main-lobe width; window-family bandwidth tables; sufficient peak-separation rules; and difference-frequency cycles.
§5.5.1, Other Definitions of Main-Lobe Width: smooth windows without zero crossings and the filter-design interpretation of passband, transition band, stopband, and sidelobe specification.
§5.5.2, Simple Sufficient Condition for Peak Resolution: separating shifted window main lobes, M >= K fs/|f2-f1|, effective width K, and empirical sharper constants K-star.

§5.5.3, Periodic Signals: harmonic spacing, driven versus freely vibrating sources, the rule M >= KP for period-P signals, and equal effective lengths across rectangular, Hamming, Blackman, and Blackman-Harris windows.

§5.5.4, Tighter Bounds for Minimum Window Length: orthogonal, stationary-point, sidelobe-matched, and full-main-lobe separation rules, with the stationary-point spacing as a near-optimal practical criterion.
§5.6, Sinusoidal Peak Interpolation: zero-padding plus quadratic interpolation as QIFFT, perceptual error tolerance, and comparison with ideal spectral interpolation.

§5.6.1, Quadratic Interpolation of Spectral Peaks: three-bin parabolic fitting in dB magnitude, closed-form peak location/height/curvature, exactness for an ideal Gaussian-window transform, phase interpolation, and Matlab implementation.
§5.6.2, Bias of Parabolic Peak Interpolation: systematic model-mismatch error, unbiased bin-centered and half-bin cases, and hybrid zero-padding/interpolation design.
§5.7, Optimal Peak-Finding in the Spectrum: the QIFFT procedure, zero-padding factors for inaudible bias, low- versus high-frequency perceptual bounds, and Matlab design calculations.

§5.7, Least-Squares Sinusoidal Parameter Estimation: complex sinusoid plus white-noise model, nonlinear/nonconvex frequency fitting, projection-based amplitude and phase estimates, and DTFT-magnitude frequency search.

§5.7, Maximum-Likelihood Sinusoid Estimation: Gaussian likelihood, equivalence with least squares, multiple well-resolved sinusoids, nonlinear optimization for overlapping peaks, prewhitening for colored noise, and the general deterministic-mean result.
Chapter 6, Spectrum Analysis of Noise: stationary stochastic-process viewpoint, autocorrelation and PSD estimation, biased/unbiased conventions, averaging, and practical audio examples.

§6.1, Introduction to Noise: tape-hiss denoising and spectral-modeling synthesis as motivating uses; finite sequences cannot reveal randomness without a model; stationary noise is treated as filtered white noise.

§§6.2–6.3, Spectral Characteristics and White Noise: random spectral phase, phase removal through magnitude-squared spectra, whiteness as lack of sample correlation rather than a particular amplitude distribution, and empirical whiteness tests.
§6.4, Sample Autocorrelation: unbiased lag-product averaging, finite-support indexing, sample variance at zero lag, convergence to the true autocorrelation, and the impulse test for white noise.
§6.5, Sample Power Spectral Density: PSD as the DTFT of autocorrelation, total area as variance, real/even symmetry, and the flat spectrum of white noise.

§§6.6–6.9, Biased, Smoothed, and Cyclic Autocorrelation/PSD Estimates: Bartlett lag weighting, asinc-squared spectral smoothing, FFT implementation with zero padding, optional mean/trend removal, and the need for ensemble/time averaging.
§6.10, Why an Impulse Is Not White Noise: deterministic frequency-flat impulse versus stationary white noise, plus a blockwise stationarity test that separates them.
§6.11, The Periodogram: normalized squared-magnitude DTFT/FFT, Bartlett-smoothed PSD interpretation, asymptotic expected value, and inconsistency caused by variance comparable to the mean.

§§6.12–6.13, Welch's Method: frame-wise periodograms, time averaging, autocorrelation counterpart, resolution–stability compromise, overlap/COLA-compatible windows, block count, and Matlab implementation.
§6.14, Filtered White Noise: colored, pink, and brown noise; autocorrelation and PSD determined by the shaping filter; moving-average and 1/f synthesis/analysis examples.
§6.15, Processing Gain: coherent sinusoidal versus noncoherent noise addition, N-fold DFT-bin SNR gain, 3 dB per doubled transform length, and the necessity of quoting SNR bandwidth.
§6.16, The Panning Problem: amplitude-preserving versus power-preserving stereo gains, frequency-dependent interaural coherence, and why equal-power panning is the practical default.
Chapter 7, Time-Frequency Displays: STFT as a sequence of local spectra, classic speech/audio spectrograms, and perceptually motivated loudness displays.
§7.1, The Short-Time Fourier Transform: goals of perceptual display and model measurement, pitch versus fundamental frequency, mathematical definition, window hop, and constant-overlap-add condition.
§7.1, Practical STFT Computation: time-normalized frames, zero-centered windows, zero-padding, FFT buffer rotation, optional phase restoration, and the window/frame/FFT/hop parameter roles.

§7.1, Dual Interpretations and Time-Frequency Distribution: overlap-add frame sequence versus downsampled uniform filter bank, and rectangular time-frequency resolution cells bounded by time-bandwidth tradeoffs.
§7.2, Classic Spectrograms: log-magnitude STFT intensity, time/frequency oversampling, parameter tuning, cochlear analogy, synthesis-model matching, and a measured speech example.
§7.2.1, Spectrogram of Speech: 20 ms Hamming analysis, fourfold spectral interpolation, phoneme localization, harmonic resolution, pitch/formant tracking, and interpretation of vocal-tract formants.

§7.3, Audio Spectrograms and Auditory Filter Banks: limits of a uniform-resolution STFT, nonuniform constant-Q/wavelet/gammatone/gamma-chirp banks, excitation patterns, critical-band sampling, and specific loudness.

§7.3.2, Loudness Spectrogram: multiresolution STFT, level- and frequency-dependent auditory interpolation kernels, nonuniform spectral resampling, excitation patterns, compressive specific loudness, and temporal loudness smoothing.

§7.3.3 examples: measured-speech MRSTFT, excitation pattern, auditory filter shapes, specific loudness, four-way display comparison, and instantaneous/short-term/long-term loudness in sones and phons.
Chapter 7 Summary: STFT-based path from classic spectrogram through auditory resampling and nonlinear compression to loudness-versus-time/frequency displays.
key_results: §5.1: A real sinusoid A cos(omega0 t+phi) is the sum of conjugate complex exponentials with coefficients (A/2)exp(±j phi); its Fourier spectrum is a conjugate pair of impulses at ±omega0.
§5.3: shifting a length-M zero-centered window by (M-1)/2 samples to make it causal multiplies its transform by exp(-j omega(M-1)/2), introducing linear phase without changing magnitude.

§5.4: windowing a complex sinusoid produces S_R(omega)=2pi W(omega-omega0); therefore every measured sinusoidal peak is exactly the analysis-window transform shifted to the tone frequency and scaled by its complex amplitude.

§5.4: the window-transform main lobe limits separation of nearby frequencies, while sidelobes limit detection of weak tones near strong tones; these are distinct failure modes requiring different window choices.

§5.4.1 examples: two sinusoids separated by Delta omega can look spuriously resolved or displaced when their window-transform lobes overlap; only the two-difference-cycle rectangular case is insensitive to the tested relative phase.
§5.5: for a length-M rectangular window, side-lobe spacing is Omega_M=2pi/M and zero-to-zero main-lobe width is 2 Omega_M=4pi/M, equivalently 2 fs/M hertz.
§5.5.2: a simple sufficient resolution requirement for a window whose main lobe spans K bins is M >= K fs/|f2-f1|—the window must span at least K cycles of the minimum difference frequency.

§5.5.2/Table 5.2: sharper empirically verified K-star values for accurate FFT-peak measurement are approximately 1.44 rectangular, 2.22 Hamming, 2.36 Hann, and 2.02 Blackman, substantially below full zero-to-zero separation.
§5.5.3: for a periodic signal with P samples per fundamental period, resolving harmonics is assured by M >= KP; differing physical window lengths can thus share the same effective resolution length.

§5.5.4: placing one peak at the first stationary point of the other's main lobe makes both derivatives vanish at the true peaks, removing first-order peak-location bias and closely approximating optimal minimum spacing.

§5.5 Summary: as a broad design rule, an analysis window should see at least about 1.5 cycles of the minimum difference frequency; tapered windows have shorter effective durations than their sample counts suggest.
§5.6.1: for dB magnitudes alpha, beta, gamma at bins -1,0,1 around a peak, the parabolic offset is p=(1/2)(alpha-gamma)/(alpha-2 beta+gamma), and the peak height is beta-(1/4)(alpha-gamma)p.

§5.6.1: quadratic interpolation is exact for an ideal Gaussian window on a dB scale because its log-magnitude transform is a parabola; other windows are locally quadratic only as a Taylor approximation.

§5.6.2: parabolic peak estimates are unbiased when the true peak is exactly on a DFT bin or halfway between bins, but generally biased elsewhere; zero-padding provides exact bandlimited spectral interpolation and controls that bias.

§5.7/Table 5.3: for peak-frequency bias below 0.1% of fs/M, minimum zero-padding factors are about 4.1 rectangular, 2.4 generalized Hamming, and 1.8 Blackman; 0.1% frequency error is normally inaudible in audio.

§5.7 low-frequency bounds/Table 5.4: below roughly 1 kHz, a fixed 1 Hz error criterion better matches frequency JND data; Blackman needs no zero padding below 125 Hz and generalized Hamming none below 62.5 Hz for one-period windows.

§5.7, amplitude/phase estimation: with known frequency, the optimal complex least-squares estimate is the normalized projection Ahat exp(j phihat)=(1/N) DTFT_omega0{x}; amplitude and phase are its magnitude and argument.
§5.7, frequency estimation: the least-squares estimate of an unknown single-sinusoid frequency maximizes |DTFT_omega{x}|; evaluating the complex projection there supplies its amplitude and phase.

§5.7, likelihood: for a deterministic sinusoid in independent zero-mean Gaussian white noise, maximizing likelihood is identical to minimizing squared residual error, so the DTFT-peak estimator is both LS and ML.

§5.7, multiple sinusoids: independent interpolated peak finding approximates ML only when peaks are well resolved and sidelobe overlap is negligible; overlapping lobes require joint nonlinear optimization over amplitudes, phases, and frequencies.

§5.7, nonwhite noise/general result: colored noise should be prewhitened before applying the white-noise estimator; more generally, ML equals LS for any deterministic mean model plus zero-mean Gaussian white noise.
Chapter 6 introduction: the PSD is the DTFT of autocorrelation, S_x(omega)=DTFT{r_x}; for zero-mean signals its integral over normalized frequency equals r_x(0), the variance/average power.
§6.4: the unbiased sample autocorrelation uses 1/(N-|l|) times the sum of available lag products; at l=0 it is sample variance, and for white noise it converges to sigma^2 delta(l).

§§6.6–6.7: ordinary finite-signal autocorrelation is the unbiased sample autocorrelation multiplied by a Bartlett window; correspondingly, its squared-magnitude spectrum is the sample PSD smoothed by an asinc-squared kernel.

§6.9: an acyclic sample autocorrelation can be computed by zero-padding an M-sample signal to FFT size N>=2M-1, taking |FFT|^2, inverse transforming, and optionally dividing out the Bartlett lag weights.
§6.10: an impulse has a flat spectrum and impulse autocorrelation but is not white noise because it is not stationary; blockwise autocorrelations expose one nonzero block followed by zero blocks.

§6.11: the periodogram P=(1/M)|DTFT{x_w}|^2 has the correct asymptotic expected value but standard deviation comparable to its mean, so increasing record length alone does not yield a stable per-band noise-level estimate.
§6.12: Welch's estimate is the arithmetic mean of K windowed-frame periodograms, Shat_x^W(omega_k)=(1/K)sum_m P_xm,M(omega_k); averaging, not merely transforming, creates statistical stability.
§6.12.2: with N_x samples, a practical default balances resolution and stability by choosing frame length M and frame count K both approximately sqrt(N_x).

§6.13: nonrectangular Welch windows should overlap so their shifts sum to a constant; typical hops are (M-1)/2 for generalized Hamming windows and about M/3 for Blackman, with K=floor((N_x-M)/R)+1 frames.
§6.14: if x=h*v and v is white with variance sigma_v^2, then r_x(l)=sigma_v^2(h star h)(l) and S_x(omega)=sigma_v^2|H(omega)|^2; all correlation/color is embodied by the shaping filter.

§6.14.1: an eight-tap moving-average process has triangular autocorrelation 8-|l| for |l|<8 and PSD sin^2(4 omega)/sin^2(omega/2), illustrating exact time/frequency dual descriptions of colored noise.

§6.14.2: ideal pink-noise PSD is proportional to 1/f and requires amplitude response proportional to 1/sqrt(f), which no finite-order rational filter realizes exactly; stable IIR approximation can nevertheless be perceptually exact.

§6.15: an N-point DFT gives N-fold processing gain for a bin-centered sinusoid in white noise: expected signal power grows as N^2 A^2 while per-bin noise grows as N sigma_v^2, adding 3 dB SNR per doubled N.
§6.15: frequency-domain SNR is meaningless without a bandwidth; narrowing a filter around a zero-bandwidth deterministic component repeatedly removes noise while retaining the signal.

§6.16: coherent equal speaker signals preserve amplitude at center with gains (1/2,1/2), while uncorrelated signals preserve power with (1/sqrt(2),1/sqrt(2)); real stereo panning commonly chooses the latter.
§7.1.1: X_m(omega)=sum_n x(n)w(n-mR)exp(-j omega n); if shifted windows satisfy sum_m w(n-mR)=1, then sum_m X_m(omega)=X(omega), the whole-signal DTFT.

§7.1.1: rectangular windows are COLA at hop M, while Bartlett and generalized Hamming windows are COLA at M/2 with proper endpoints; COLA is essential for artifact-free reconstruction but can be relaxed for display-only analysis.

§7.1.2: with window length M and FFT length N>=M, frequency sampling is information-preserving because the windowed frame is time limited; zero-padding factor N/M is the ideal spectral interpolation factor.

§7.1.3: the STFT is simultaneously a time sequence of local Fourier transforms and a bank of frequency-shifted lowpass filters whose outputs are downsampled by hop R; the window is each channel's anti-aliasing impulse response.
§7.1.4: an STFT tiles time-frequency space with uniform rectangular resolution cells; window length and type set the cell aspect ratio and area, bounded below by a time-bandwidth uncertainty product.

§7.2: a classic spectrogram is a log-magnitude intensity plot of the STFT; M controls frequency resolution, window type controls sidelobes, N controls frequency interpolation, and R controls time-axis sampling.

§7.2.1: a 20 ms speech window is short enough to localize most frames within one phoneme yet long enough to contain at least two periods of a 100 Hz voiced fundamental, balancing harmonic resolution with tracking of pitch and formants.

§7.3.1: an auditory filter bank is a nonuniform frequency sampler; each auditory-filter response acts as a frequency-dependent interpolation kernel, and its output power defines the excitation pattern.
§7.3.2: a loudness spectrogram pipeline combines multiresolution STFT, auditory-filter resampling, and a level/frequency-dependent compressive nonlinearity to produce specific loudness per ERB.
§7.3.2: instantaneous loudness is the sum of specific loudness across frequency; short- and long-term loudness apply asymmetric temporal smoothing that rises quickly and decays more slowly.

§7.3.3: spectral smoothing by auditory kernels shortens effective time windows, so the maximum safe hop must be re-evaluated from the combined window or widest auditory-filter bandwidth rather than inherited blindly from the original MRSTFT.
pedagogy: This shard is application-first but mathematically explicit. Smith starts Chapter 5 with what sinusoidal peaks buy in audio—compact additive models, pitch tracking, source grouping, restoration—then builds every formula from a visible shifted window transform. Controlled two-tone plots turn resolution into an experiment before main-lobe constants and sufficient bounds are derived. The next progression is equally deliberate: three-bin interpolation becomes QIFFT; QIFFT becomes orthogonal projection; DTFT peak search becomes least squares; a Gaussian likelihood finally shows why the same estimator is maximum likelihood. Chapter 6 repeatedly warns that randomness is a model imposed on finite data. It alternates lag- and frequency-domain views, derives each normalization and bias, then uses executable Matlab snippets and pink-noise experiments to make stability, averaging, and processing gain tangible. Chapter 7 converts those local spectra into time-frequency displays and then critiques the uniform STFT against hearing, ending in a full psychoacoustic pipeline applied to one speech recording. Proof style is constructive rather than theorem-heavy: convolution identities, projection geometry, likelihood algebra, expected powers, and COLA sums terminate in a design rule or implementation. There are no conventional end-of-chapter exercises in these chapters; parameter sweeps, worked numerical tables, short Matlab/Octave programs, and paired plots function as laboratories. Prerequisites are complex exponentials, DTFT/DFT/FFT, convolution/correlation, analysis windows, elementary calculus and linear algebra, probability/Gaussian noise, and basic audio/perception vocabulary.

gems: Sinusoidal models are called 'unreasonably effective' for tonal sound: the ear weights short-time spectral peaks so strongly that a sparse set of tracked peak parameters supports synthesis, calibration, pitch detection, source grouping, and tape-hiss rejection. [Chapter 5 introduction]

The same two tones can look resolved with a half difference-frequency cycle when placed in phase quadrature, yet the apparent peaks sit at the wrong frequencies. The example turns 'two bumps' from a visual judgment into a warning about estimator bias. [§5.4.1, Figs. 5.8–5.9]

Smith's memorable resolution unit is not FFT bins but cycles of the difference frequency: a window generally needs to see about 1.5 cycles, while full-main-lobe separation gives a conservative window-specific K-cycle rule. [§§5.5.2–5.5 Summary]

A 300-sample Blackman window, 200-sample Hamming window, and 100-sample rectangular window can all have roughly the same effective two-period resolving length; the discarded edge weight is made visible as lost effective duration. [§5.5.3, Fig. 5.13]

The stationary-point separation rule explains resolution through derivatives: put each peak over a stationary point of the other lobe and neither peak sits on a slope, eliminating first-order frequency bias. [§5.5.4, Fig. 5.14(b)]

Three adjacent dB bins are enough for a closed-form frequency and amplitude correction, and the method is exactly right for the conceptual Gaussian window because its log spectrum is already a parabola. [§5.6.1, Fig. 5.15]

The source quantifies 'perceptually exact' rather than leaving it rhetorical: 0.1% tuning error is generally inaudible, and Blackman needs only 1.8x zero padding for that bound, versus 4.1x rectangular. [§5.7, Table 5.3]

Low-frequency pitch acuity changes the engineering specification itself: below about 1 kHz, a fixed 1 Hz bound is more appropriate than a percentage, and some tapered windows need no zero padding at the lowest tested frequencies. [§5.7, Table 5.4]

QIFFT is not presented as a clever hack: orthogonal projection and Gaussian likelihood lead back to the same DTFT peak, making modest zero-padding plus parabolic interpolation a fast approximation to the actual LS/ML estimator. [§§5.6–5.7]

A finite list of random-looking numbers cannot prove randomness. Smith discloses that his eight-number example came from Matlab only after using it to insist that every noise analysis is ultimately a model fitted to data. [§6.1.2 What Is Noise?]

An impulse and white noise both contain every frequency equally, but only the noise is stationary. Splitting the record into blocks makes the distinction immediate: one impulse block followed by zeros can never look statistically comparable. [§6.10]

The periodogram has the right expected value yet the wrong temperament: its standard deviation is comparable to its mean. Welch averaging is therefore not cosmetic smoothing but the operation that turns random band values into a usable noise-level estimate. [§§6.11–6.12]

Pink-noise synthesis is a productive impossibility: no finite rational filter exactly realizes 1/sqrt(f) amplitude response, yet a short stable IIR approximation can be perceptually exact and then verified against the -3 dB/octave law. [§§6.14.2–6.14.3]

Processing gain is pictured as a coordinate change: sinusoidal energy piles into one DFT coordinate while noise stays spread everywhere, yielding N-fold SNR gain and 3 dB per doubled transform length. [§6.15]

The stereo-center gain has two correct answers. Coherent low frequencies want one-half per speaker; decorrelated energy wants one over square-root two. The standard equal-power pan law is a concession to frequency and listener geometry. [§6.16]

Smith separates pitch from fundamental frequency: when partials are stretched, perceived pitch may be a compromise frequency that is not physically present, while fundamental-frequency estimation remains a model-measurement problem. [§7.1]

COLA is treated with appropriate severity: violating it can create processing artifacts, but for a display-only spectrogram the same violation merely weights some time samples less, so 'nothing disastrous happens.' [§7.1.1]

The 20 ms speech window earns its canonical status with two simultaneous facts: it usually stays within one phoneme and still spans two periods of a 100 Hz voice, balancing event tracking against harmonic separation. [§7.2.1, Fig. 7.2]

The loudness-spectrogram sequence makes perception an inspectable algorithm: multiple FFT resolutions become ERB-spaced excitation, then compression becomes specific loudness, all applied to exactly the same speech utterance. [§7.3.3, Figs. 7.4–7.8]

The excitation-pattern plot reveals only four or five voiced harmonics but sharp pitch pulses at higher ERBs, while formants become clearer around 25 ERBs—a concrete demonstration that an auditory representation reorganizes, not merely smooths, spectral evidence. [§7.3.3, Fig. 7.5]
